title: Into the wheel
hookLine: a young warrior knows how to break into the wheel formation, and says out loud that he doesn't know the way out
carry: tradition says a child listens before birth
tomorrow: alone inside the wheel. what does Abhimanyu do now?

cards: Morning, and across the field Drona has arranged his army into a shape the Pandavas dread: the chakra, the wheel. Ring inside ring of chariots, elephants and warriors, turning to close around anyone who comes near.
On the Pandava side, only a few know how to break it. Arjuna knows. Krishna knows.

And Arjuna is far away on the other side of the field, answering the sworn ones' challenge, just as the plan intended. Yudhishthira looks around and finds one more person who might know: Arjuna's son, Abhimanyu.

teach.h: I KNOW THE WAY IN, NOT OUT
teach.b: Abhimanyu is the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, Krishna's sister: young, fearless, already a fine warrior. Yudhishthira asks him to break the wheel, and his answer is honest.
In Ganguli's telling, he can pierce the formation, but if trouble comes he can't come out again. Bhima promises they'll follow through his gap.
So Abhimanyu drives in, breaks the ring, and he's inside, fighting brilliantly.
But behind him Jayadratha, king of Sindhu, rides into the breach. The text says he once won a gift from Shiva: for one day he could hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna. This is that day.
The wheel closes, with one young man inside. Now the part so many Hindu families add.

In the popular retelling, Abhimanyu learned the way in before he was born: Arjuna explained the wheel to Subhadra while she carried him, and she fell asleep before the way out. That isn't in the epic's own passage here.
But it rests on something Hindu tradition really holds: a child is listening before birth.
The Bhagavata Purana says Prahlada learned devotion to Vishnu inside his mother's womb, hearing the sage Narada teach her.
Hindu tradition also keeps some life-rites, the samskaras, before birth, and many Hindu families today sing bhajans and play mantras for a baby on the way.
Abhimanyu's half-heard lesson is the sad side of the same belief: what a child hears early, they carry into the wheel.

how: Abhimanyu's entry into the chakravyuha is told in the Drona Parva and retold in dance, theater and storytelling, and many Hindu families tell the popular version in which he learned the way in while still in the womb.

he said plainly he knew the way in, but not the way out.

Jayadratha held the breach, and they couldn't follow him in.

games.q: a friend says the Abhimanyu womb story proves the Mahabharata is just a fairy tale. what's the most accurate answer?
o: the womb story is a beloved addition, not in the epic's own passage, but it rests on an old Hindu belief that a child listens before birth.
it's word for word in the oldest Sanskrit text.
nobody in Hinduism thinks a baby can hear anything before birth.
games.why: the epic passage has Abhimanyu say what he knows and doesn't; the womb story came later, and leans on a real teaching: the Bhagavata's Prahlada also learned in the womb.

practice: Many Hindus begin and end their prayers with one sound, Om. Breathe in deeply. On the way out, let a low Om hum through your chest, and feel it in your bones before you hear it.
Do it three times. Then bring to mind a child you love, or the child you once were, and wish them good things to hear. If you pray, let the Om be your prayer.
If you don't, let it simply be a sound you give to someone small.
